text: Your process is stable. Every point inside the control limits. So why are results still falling outside specification?
Our lab turnaround looks steady on the chart. But the clinicians still complain. Is it good enough, or not?
That question has a number. Two, actually. Cp and Cpk. And in the Lean Six Sigma toolkit, the Process Capability Studio explains them with one simple picture: a car in a garage.

The left wall is your lower specification limit. The right wall, your upper limit. Now park the car again and again. It never stops in exactly the same place. That band of parking positions is your process spread, six sigma wide.
And notice the careful point the poster makes. The band is where many cars park over time. It is not the width of one car. Capability is about variation, never a single result.
Cp asks: could it fit? Specification width, U S L minus L S L, divided by six sigma within. It compares the size of the garage with the size of the spread.
Cpk asks the harder question: does it fit, where it actually is? It takes the distance from the mean to the nearer wall, divided by three sigma. The smaller side wins.
Watch it in three dimensions. Lower limit zero, upper limit twelve, mean six, sigma one. Cp two. Cpk two. Perfectly centred.
Now move the mean to nine. Same spread, so Cp stays at two. But the car is now close to the right wall. Cpk falls to one. The process could fit. It just isn't parked in the middle.
Part two of the Studio turns this into a decision. Move it, tighten it, or change the limits? Predict what happens to Cp and Cpk, then check every step of the working.

And an honest warning, right on the poster. Changing a specification needs legitimate customer, engineering or clinical justification. Cp and Cpk measure fit to the limits. They do not judge whether the limits are clinically right.
Then do it with real numbers. Enter your data, and the toolkit draws the capability histogram against your specification, with the fitted normal curve.
Cp one point five four. Cpk one point four nine. The chart reads itself to you: the spread could fit, the process is capable, and to improve, reduce variation. Then monitor it with a control chart.
So is that good? A Cpk of one point three three is a common minimum in industry. It leaves one extra sigma of margin inside the limits.

And the Studio tells you where it came from. Capability ratios spread through Japanese manufacturing in the nineteen seventies, and appeared in Juran's handbook. In nineteen eighty six, Victor Kane's paper formalised Cp and Cpk.
So our turnaround is stable, but not centred. We don't need to work harder. We need to move the mean.
